title: Sell Mineral Rights in Joffre, PA
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Joffre, PA
metaDescription: Joffre is a small former mining patch in Washington County, PA. See what that history means for mineral ownership and today's Marcellus values.
heroLead: Joffre is one of the small unincorporated patch towns scattered through Washington County, built originally around coal mining rather than gas.
intro: Patch towns like Joffre were built by coal companies to house miners, with company-owned rows of houses and, often, mineral reservations written into every deed the company ever sold off. When those coal operations wound down and the houses eventually sold to private owners, the mineral rights frequently stayed behind with whatever company or its successor held them — which is exactly the kind of tangled title we untangle for families trying to figure out what they actually own around Joffre today.

sections.heading: Patch-Town Deeds Are Their Own Category
paragraphs: Because Joffre grew up around a specific coal operation, its property records often reference old corporate names that don't exist anymore, having been absorbed through decades of mergers. Tracing a mineral reservation back to its current owner in a patch town like this takes real courthouse work, but it's very doable with patience and the right search of the Washington County records in the county seat.

sections.heading: Washington County's Wet-Gas Standing
paragraphs: Washington County is core Marcellus wet-gas territory, among the most actively drilled counties in the entire play. That activity level around Joffre means even a modest, oddly-shaped patch-town parcel can sit inside a producing or planned drilling unit, which is worth checking before assuming a small property has nothing to offer.

sections.heading: What We Look for on a Joffre Property
paragraphs: We start by identifying whether the coal-era deed severed oil and gas along with coal, or left gas with the surface. From there we check current unit filings and any nearby royalty activity. Depending on what surfaces, we put together an honest range rather than assuming a small patch-town lot is worth little just because of its size.

faqs.question: Our deed only mentions a coal company from the 1920s — does that cover gas too?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the exact language used, which is why we pull and read the original deed rather than assuming based on the era it was written.

faqs.question: Is a small patch-town lot even worth checking?
faqs.answer: Lot size doesn't determine whether minerals were severed or what a unit interest might be worth — Washington County activity levels matter more than acreage alone.

faqs.question: How do we prove ownership if the original company is gone?
faqs.answer: We trace the corporate succession through recorded assignments and, where needed, work with a title attorney to document the current chain of ownership.
